May Have and Might Have can be used to speculate about the past.
You can use “May Have” and “Might Have” to express past uncertainty.
I suppose I may have been a bit tough on her.
You can use “Might Have” to refer to a past possibility which did not occur.
My goodness, you might have lost everything!
You can use both in negative statements to express uncertainty.
She might not have received my text.
“Might Have” is also used to express annoyance, especially at someone's failure to say or do something.
You might have told me that your parents were visiting!
Finally, “Might Have” is used idiomatically with “Known” to express something that should have been obvious or expected.
I might have known she would try to pull something. She's always been a prankster.

You use relative clauses to give extra information about someone or something. There are two types of relative clauses: “Defining” and “Non-Defining”.
A “Defining Relative Clause” tells you which specific person or thing you are talking about.

The kid who delivers the newspaper wanted a tip.
The newspaper which the kid delivers is called “The Times”.
The bike that he rides is red.

A “Non-Defining Relative Clause” tells you extra information regarding the person or thing you are talking about. This information is usually not essential.

For example:

The kid, who went to the same school as my brother, delivered the newspaper.
The newspaper, which is printed in town, is called “The Times”.
Note that the relative pronoun “that” is not used in Non-Defining Relative Clauses.

images.text:
Water is both a source of life and a powerful force. Ever since the story of Noah, who built a famous ark for the great flood, people have been struggling to control the world's waterways and prevent their flooding. Major rivers which bring the gifts of precious water and fertile soil to the people who live along their banks also bring disaster. What might have happened if people had known how to control water more efficiently?
It's hard to say. Throughout human history, people have struggled to control the raging waters of major waterways but never with complete success. The Chinese who live along the Yellow River have had more than two thousand years of trying to control the watery, and at times, angry giant.

In the third century BC an engineer named Wu, who later became the Emperor of China, designed and executed a successful plan to drain the mighty Yellow River, causing the water level to drop. Despite Wu's success, the Yellow River has flooded more than one thousand times in the last two thousand years and caused the deaths of over seven million people in the last hundred years alone. How many more people might have died if Wu had not been able to drain the river?
The present Chinese government, which continues to struggle against the three thousand miles of the Yellow River, is presently at work constructing a major dam to further control this fluid dragon.

In the U.S. there are problems with flooding as well, as seen when Hurricane Katrina hit land.
What might have happened if New Orleans had been more prepared for the flooding, which caused 108 billion dollars in damage and killed thousands?  Rising flood waters may not have caused businesses to close, homes to be destroyed or families to be evacuated. A state of emergency may not have been declared. The levees, which were supposed to keep the water out, failed. New Orleans, which is well below sea level and sinking, is expecting more flooding in the future. The levees, which can erode over time, are being raised. Nevertheless, will they hold when the water rises again?
